ta-l1d34q3-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the third question of Distinction 34 turns to what is said of God metaphorically and announces two articles: whether anything should be said of God metaphorically, and from what things God should be named metaphorically.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e109.summary: First argument that nothing should be said of God metaphorically. Boethius says in divine matters one must proceed intellectually and not be led to imagination, and metaphors are taken from imaginations of sensibles.
claims: Divine matters require intellect, not imagination.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e112.summary: Second argument. All who transfer names do so by some likeness (the Philosopher), and likeness is the same quality in different things (Boethius), but bodily qualities are not in God.
claims: Likeness requires shared quality.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e115.summary: Third argument. All teaching, especially Scripture, aims to manifest truth, and metaphors or symbolic locutions are veils of truth (Dionysius).
claims: Metaphors veil truth.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument. Knowledge comes by assimilation of intellect to thing, and our intellect, being immaterial, is more like divine than bodily things, so divine things should not be shown us through bodily likenesses.
claims: The intellect is more like divine things.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e122.summary: Sed contra from Dionysius: the divine ray cannot shine on us except veiled in a variety of likenesses, and the divine ray is the truth of divine things.
claims: Divine truth reaches us veiled in likenesses.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e128.summary: Thomas's determination. It is most fitting that divine things be signified to us by bodily likenesses, for four reasons. First and principally, the height of the matter exceeds our intellect's capacity, so it must be proposed in our mode, and it is connatural to us to go from sensibles to intelligibles and from posterior to prior, so intelligibles are proposed under sensible figures, that the mind may rise from the known to the unknown. Second, since we have both intellective and sensitive knowing powers, divine wisdom provided that both be led back to divine things as far as possible, using bodily figures the sensitive part can grasp, since it could not reach the intelligible content. Third, we know more truly what God is not than what he is (Dionysius: affirmations about God are unfitted, negations true), and since everything said of God fits him not as in creatures but by some imitation and likeness, his eminence is shown more expressly by removing from him the more manifest things, which are bodily, so that the mind, accustomed to these, learns to attribute nothing to God except by likeness, as the creature imitates the Creator. Fourth, the hiding of divine truth: the depths of faith must be hidden from unbelievers, lest they mock, and from the simple, lest they err. All these are given by Dionysius at the start of the Celestial Hierarchy and in the letter to Titus.
claims: Metaphor fits theology because we rise from sensibles, because sense too is led to God, because bodily images show God's transcendence by negation, and because truth must be hidden from mockers and the simple.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e131.summary: Reply to the first argument. In knowledge of intelligibles there is the starting point of speculation and its end. The start is from sensibles, the end in intelligibles, as in natural knowledge we take universal intentions from sense species by the agent intellect's light. So, as to the end of speculation, the start must rise from sensible species to divine things.
claims: Speculation starts from sensibles and ends in intelligibles.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e134.summary: Reply to the second argument. Likeness is twofold: by participation in the same form, which bodily things do not have with God; and of proportionality, the same relation of proportions (eight to four as six to three; a consul to a city as a pilot to a ship). Transfer from bodily to divine things is by the second: God is called fire because, as fire makes melted things flow by its heat, God by his goodness pours perfections into all creatures.
claims: Metaphor rests on likeness of proportionality, not shared form.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e137.summary: Reply to the third argument. Truth should be manifested in proportion to the recipients, and since for some its manifestation would harm rather than help, attacking it from impiety or failing from simplicity, divine truth is to be hidden (Matt. 7:6, 'do not give what is holy to dogs').
claims: Truth is manifested in proportion to recipients.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e144.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. There is assimilation by agreement in nature, by which our intellect is more like divine than sensible things, but this is not what knowledge requires. Knowledge requires assimilation by information, as sight is assimilated to colour by the pupil's being informed by its species, and the intellect, by the way of nature, is informed only by species abstracted from sense (the Philosopher: as colour to sight, so phantasms to intellect), so in this way the intellect is more assimilated to sensibles than to divine things.
claims: Knowing requires informing species, which for us come from sense.
concepts: assimilation by nature vs. by information

ta-l1d34q3-d1e156.summary: First argument that metaphors should not be taken from base things. All transfer is by likeness, and base things lack the noble conditions from which a likeness to God could be drawn.
claims: Base things lack noble likeness.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e159.summary: Second argument, against the reply that even the basest things bear some likeness to divine goodness as vestiges. Every creature has the likeness of vestige or image, so metaphors could be taken from all creatures, which is not found.
claims: Vestige would license all creatures.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e162.summary: Third argument. Divine goodness is more expressly reflected in incorporeal than sensible things, so angels' names should rather be transferred to God.
claims: Angelic names would fit better.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e166.summary: Fourth argument. Wholly different things should not be expressed by the same figures, but some figures, like serpent and lion, designate contrary powers, so at least these should not be transferred to God.
claims: Serpent and lion designate evil powers.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e169.summary: Sed contra. Scripture often transfers even names of brute animals to God, as Hos. 13:7, 'I will be to them like a lioness, like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians'.
claims: Scripture uses animal images of God.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e175.summary: Thomas's determination. Dionysius (Celestial Hierarchy 2) shows that divine things are signified to us even more fittingly through baser creatures than nobler ones. First, they hide divine things more, which is needed. Second, they are further from God, and since the most fitting mode of signifying God is by negation, these likenesses are more fitting. Third, for our benefit: base figures give less occasion of error, since no one doubts that God cannot properly be some base animal, so Scripture plainly does not attribute such things properly, whereas the simple, who can hardly think beyond sensibles, might easily think the noblest bodies properly fit God if said of him, so likenesses from baser things draw the mind from error by their very quality. Still, Scripture also signifies God by noble creatures, like the sun and a star, though less often.
claims: Base images fit divine signification better: they hide, they negate, and they do not mislead.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e178.summary: Reply to the first argument. According to Dionysius nothing wholly lacks participation in divine goodness, so fitting likenesses can be taken from even the basest things.
claims: Everything participates divine goodness.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e181.summary: Reply to the second argument. Some creature names name not only what is created but an attached defect of guilt, as 'devil' names a nature deformed by sin, and such names cannot be transferred to God.
claims: Names implying guilt cannot be transferred to God.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e184.summary: Reply to the third argument. In spiritual creatures one can consider the perfections of divine goodness in themselves, by which God is named properly, not symbolically, as wise and understanding (Liber de causis: God is named by the name of his first effect, intelligence); or the determinate mode of participating them, belonging to a determinate angelic nature or order, whose names cannot be said of God properly or even metaphorically, since metaphor must be taken from what is manifest to sense. So God is never named Cherubim or Seraphim in Scripture, as he is named lion or bear.
claims: Spiritual perfections are said properly of God; angelic modes neither properly nor metaphorically.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e188.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. One thing has different properties, so nothing prevents transferring it to contraries by different properties: God is called lion for liberality or strength, the devil for cruelty. Sometimes too (Dionysius to Titus) the same name signifies the participant, the participation, and its principle, as 'fire' may name a man with charity, charity itself, and God infusing charity, each to be expounded differently.
claims: One image can signify contraries by different properties.

ta-l1d34q3-d1e197.summary: An expositio textus. (1) The heretics' argument (the essence that is the Father is the Son, so the same thing is Father and Son, begets and is begotten) turns on the equivocation of 'thing': taken essentially, the essence is one thing that neither begets nor is begotten, nor is Father or Son adjectivally; taken personally, it is not one thing but three, one begetting, one begotten, one proceeding, though the essence itself neither begets, is begotten, nor proceeds. (2) Hilary proves Father and Son are of one nature from Rom. 8, which names one Spirit of Father and Son: if 'spirit' is taken essentially, one spirit means one nature; if personally, the Holy Spirit is from Father and Son, and nothing of one nature is from things of different natures, so Father and Son are of one nature; hence 'distinguish, heretic, the Spirit of Christ from the Spirit of God', which cannot be done. (3) 'God and what is God's are not the same' can be read as a reductio (if it were in God as in creatures, what is God's would not be God) or absolutely, meaning they are not the same in concept. (4) 'Man began to think it is in the Creator as he saw in creatures, from which these names were transferred' seems against Eph. 3:15 ('from whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named'); as to the thing signified paternity is prior in God, but as to the mode of signifying of our imposed name it fits creatures first and is transferred to God.
claims: The heretics' argument equivocates on 'res'.
Paternity is prior in God as to the thing signified and in creatures as to the name's imposition.
concepts: prior in God, posterior in naming

ta-l1d34q3-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces two articles on metaphorical names: whether God should be named metaphorically, and from what things.

ta-l1d34q3-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that it is most fitting to signify God by bodily likenesses. We rise from sensibles to intelligibles, sense too should be led to God, bodily images show God's transcendence by negation, and divine truth must be hidden from mockers and the simple. Speculation starts from sensibles and ends in intelligibles, metaphor rests on likeness of proportionality, truth is manifested in proportion to recipients, and knowing requires species from sense.
claims: Metaphor fits theology for epistemic, negative, and protective reasons.
Metaphor rests on proportionality, not shared form.

ta-l1d34q3-Dd1e148.summary: Article 2, following Dionysius, holds that base creatures signify God even more fittingly than noble ones, since they hide more, negate more, and mislead less. Everything participates divine goodness, but names implying guilt cannot be transferred. Spiritual perfections are said properly, angelic modes not at all, and one image can signify contraries by different properties.
claims: Base images signify God more fittingly than noble ones.

ta-l1d34q3-Dd1e192.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 34 resolves the heretics' argument by the equivocation of 'thing' and explains Hilary's proof of one nature from the one Spirit of Father and Son. It reconciles the transfer of names from creatures with Eph. 3:15: prior in God as to the thing signified, prior in creatures as to the name.
claims: The heretics equivocate on 'res'; names are prior in God as to reality.

ta-l1d34q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 34 treats metaphorical names of God. Article 1 holds that signifying God by bodily likenesses is most fitting, since we rise from sensibles, sense too is led to God, bodily images show his transcendence by negation, and truth must be hidden from the unworthy, with metaphor resting on likeness of proportionality. Article 2 holds, with Dionysius, that base creatures signify God even more fittingly than noble ones, though names implying guilt or angelic modes are excluded.
claims: Metaphor is fitting in theology and rests on proportionality.
Base images signify God more fittingly than noble ones.
